rules.why: The finding of abnormally hyperintense spinal cord white matter is compatible with several candidates, but does not specifically distinguish between them.

effects.candidate: Cervical Spinal Cord Injury with Spinal Cord Compression
effects.why: Evidence from E1, E2, and E3 suggests that MRI of the cervical spine is useful in evaluating spinal cord injuries, particularly those involving trauma.

effects.candidate: Thoracic Spinal Cord Injury with Spinal Cord Compression
effects.why: While E4 mentions the use of MRI in diagnosing spinal cord disorders, it does not specifically distinguish thoracic spinal cord injuries from other conditions.

effects.candidate: Lumbar Spinal Cord Injury with Spinal Cord Compression
effects.why: There is no direct evidence provided for lumbar spinal cord injuries in relation to MRI findings.

effects.candidate: Spinal Cord Injury without Spinal Cord Compression
effects.why: E3 discusses a case of spinal cord injury without radiological abnormality, but does not specifically address the role of MRI in such cases.

effects.candidate: Extradural Spinal Cord Compression
effects.why: Evidence from E5, E6, E7, and E8 indicates that MRI can help diagnose extradural spinal cord compression, particularly in cases involving tumors or other space-occupying lesions.

effects.candidate: Intradural Spinal Cord Compression
effects.why: E9, E10, E11, and E12 provide evidence that MRI is useful in diagnosing intradural spinal cord compression, including cases of neurenteric cysts and intradural extramedullary tuberculoma.

effects.candidate: Spinal Cord Compression due to Degenerative Disease
effects.why: While E13, E14, and E15 mention the use of imaging in evaluating spinal conditions, they do not specifically address the diagnostic utility of MRI in spinal cord compression due to degenerative disease.

effects.candidate: Other Causes of Spinal Cord Compression
effects.why: E16 provides a case report of MALT lymphoma causing spinal cord compression, but does not offer broad insights into the role of MRI in diagnosing other causes of spinal cord compression.

effects.candidate: Multiple Sclerosis-related Acute Transverse Myelitis
effects.why: Evidence from E17, E18, E19, and E20 suggests that MRI is crucial in diagnosing acute transverse myelitis, including cases related to multiple sclerosis.

effects.candidate: Idiopathic Acute Transverse Myelitis
effects.why: While E19 and E20 discuss acute transverse myelitis, they do not specifically differentiate idiopathic cases from those related to multiple sclerosis or other conditions.

effects.candidate: Post-infectious Acute Transverse Myelitis
effects.why: There is no direct evidence provided for post-infectious acute transverse myelitis in relation to MRI findings.

effects.candidate: Acute Transverse Myelitis due to Other Causes
effects.why: E27 discusses a case of extensive longitudinal transverse myelitis following vaccination, but does not broadly address the role of MRI in diagnosing acute transverse myelitis due to other causes.

effects.candidate: Viral Meningitis
effects.why: There is no direct evidence provided for viral meningitis in relation to MRI findings of the cervical spine.

effects.candidate: Bacterial Meningitis
effects.why: While E25 and E26 discuss bacterial meningitis, they do not specifically address the role of MRI in diagnosing this condition.

effects.candidate: Inflammatory Disorder (e.g. Transverse Myelitis)
effects.why: E27 provides evidence that MRI can be used to diagnose inflammatory disorders such as transverse myelitis.

effects.candidate: Other Infectious or Inflammatory Disorders
effects.why: E28 and E29 mention the use of imaging in evaluating infectious and inflammatory disorders, but do not specifically address the diagnostic utility of MRI in these conditions.

effects.candidate: Acute Spinal Cord Injury from Non-traumatic Causes
effects.why: While E31, E32, and E33 discuss spinal cord injuries and the use of imaging, they do not specifically focus on non-traumatic causes or the diagnostic role of MRI in these cases.

effects.candidate: Spontaneous Spinal Epidural Hematoma
effects.why: Evidence from E35 and E36 indicates that MRI can be used to diagnose spontaneous spinal epidural hematoma.

effects.candidate: Acute Transverse Myelitis from Other Causes
effects.why: E27 discusses a case of transverse myelitis, but does not broadly address the role of MRI in diagnosing acute transverse myelitis from other causes.

effects.candidate: Other Rare Causes of Acute Quadriplegia
effects.why: While E37, E38, E39, and E40 mention rare causes of neurological symptoms, they do not specifically address the diagnostic utility of MRI in other rare causes of acute quadriplegia.
